:::{#def-dot-product}
#### Dot product
For any two real-valued vectors $\vx = (x_1, \ldots, x_p)$ and $\vy = (y_1, \ldots, y_p)$
of the same length $p$,
the **dot product** of $\vx$ and $\vy$ is:

$$\vx \cdot \vy = \vx\' \vy \eqdef \sumip x_i y_i$$ {#eq-inner-product}

:::

::: notes
See also the definitions in:

- @dobson4e, Section 1.3 (equation 1.1, page 7)

- @mosaiccalc, chapter on vectors

- [wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_combination)

The dot product has a different generalization for two matrices;
see [wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dot_product#Dyadics_and_matrices) for more.
:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-dot-product}
#### A dot product

For $\vx = (1, 2, 3)$ and $\vy = (4, 5, 6)$:

$$
\ba
\vx \cdot \vy
&= 1 \cd 4 + 2 \cd 5 + 3 \cd 6
&& \text{(definition of the dot product)}
\\
&= 4 + 10 + 18
&& \text{(multiply)}
\\
&= 32
&& \text{(add)}
\ea
$$

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#def-linear-combination}
#### Linear combination

A **linear combination** of the numbers $a_1, \ldots, a_k$
with **coefficients** $c_1, \ldots, c_k$
is the weighted sum

$$c_1 a_1 + \cdots + c_k a_k = \sum_{i=1}^k c_i a_i$$

A linear combination of vectors $\vecf{v}_1, \ldots, \vecf{v}_k$ of the same length
is defined entry by entry:
entry $j$ of $\sum_{i=1}^k c_i \vecf{v}_i$ is the linear combination
of the $j$th entries of $\vecf{v}_1, \ldots, \vecf{v}_k$
with the same coefficients.
For example, the linear combination of $\tp{(1, 0)}$ and $\tp{(0, 1)}$
with coefficients $2$ and $3$ is
$\tp{(2 \cd 1 + 3 \cd 0,\ 2 \cd 0 + 3 \cd 1)} = \tp{(2, 3)}$.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#rem-dot-product-lincom}
#### The dot product is a linear combination

The dot product $\vx \cdot \vy$ is a linear combination (@def-linear-combination)
of the entries of $\vy$, with coefficients $x_1, \ldots, x_p$.
In @exm-dot-product, $\vx \cdot \vy = 1 \cd 4 + 2 \cd 5 + 3 \cd 6$
is the linear combination of $4$, $5$, and $6$
with coefficients $1$, $2$, and $3$.

The dot product is also the standard *inner product* on $\reals^p$;
"inner product" is the general notion (@def-inner-product, later on this page),
of which the dot product is one example.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#thm-lincom-symmetric}
#### Dot product is symmetric

The dot product is symmetric:

$$\vx \cdot \vy = \vy \cdot \vx$$

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

::: proof

$$
\ba
\vx \cdot \vy
&= \sumip x_i y_i
&& \text{(definition of the dot product)}
\\
&= \sumip y_i x_i
&& \text{(products of numbers are symmetric)}
\\
&= \vy \cdot \vx
&& \text{(definition of the dot product)}
\ea
$$

:::
